newsitem.title: USA: CBOT soybeans end lower on weak grains, weather.
newsitem.headline: CBOT soybeans end lower on weak grains, weather.

text.p: CBOT soybean futures lost steam in late trading Thursday and ended lower on spillover weakness from grains and on ideas weather patterns were conducive to crop planting and development, traders said.

"We had a really strong reaction to the export sales and the crush," said Bill Biedermann, analyst with Allendale Inc. "Then the corn and the wheat markets, which are more focused on the weather, reacted negatively to the forecasts. If it weren't for the grains, beans may have been 20 higher."
USDA on Thursday put weekly export sales at 278,800 tonnes, above expectations for 100,000 to 200,000 tonnes.

Traders said the export figures have been a litmus test for soybean demand in recent weeks as the market tries to determine whether prices have risen enough to ration usage. The export data suggested recent price losses were too steep.
"By lowering the price, we've intensified the (tight stocks) problem," Biedermann added. "But it's a holiday weekend and speculators typically get out ahead of a holiday."
Soybeans ended 2-1/4 to 3/4 cent per bushel lower with July down 3/4 at $8.46-1/2.
July had traded as high as $8.59 but quickly fell below the 50-day moving average of $8.57-3/4, chartists noted.
The U.S. Census crush data showed usage in that area was also high, traders said. Census put April crushings at 114.757 million bushels, above expectations for 113.125 million.

News late Wednesday that Argentina's Agricultural Secretariat cut its soybean crop projection to 11.5 million tonnes from 12.86 million was also deemed supportive. Trade sources had expected a one million-tonne cut.

Technically, chartists called the opening trade bullish because the July contract pushed above the 50-day moving average level at $8.57-3/4 per bushel. But the late sell off took out support at $8.50 for the second straight day, setting the market up for more losses, they said.
Weather forecasts weighed on new crop months most of the session as trade sources continued to draw parallels between this year's growing conditions and 1994 when U.S. farmers produced bumper crops.

Forecasts called for a brief weekend warmup, followed by more cool, wet weather for much of the U.S. Midwest. While some trade sources said the below-normal temperatures would slow development, others noted 1994 was also a cool year.

On the day, Merrill Lynch and Prudential Securities each sold three million bushels July while Refco Inc bought three million July, traders said. Produce Grain spread 2.5 million July/August at 31 cents, premium July. In options trade, Lind-Waldock bought 500 July $8.25 puts at 8-1/4 to 8-1/2 cents and sold 500 July $8.00 puts at three cents. Continental Grain sold 200 July $8.75 calls at 12-3/4.
Soybean futures volume was estimated by CBOT at 55,000 contracts, compared with Wednesday's actual volume of 64,372.
